title: TCA, FormEngine, and Backend Forms
hints: TCA changes can affect persisted data, editor workflows, and generated backend forms.
Prefer established TCA option names and existing FormEngine behavior.
Add functional coverage for TCA processing, data providers, or backend form rendering behavior.

A new field or option is user-facing, so it needs its labels in the same change — the field label, and the item labels of a select. An unlabelled field renders its own key to the editor. typo3_label_lookup says which trans-units the installation already has.

title: Adding a Field to a Core Palette
appliesTo: field is missing from the backend form
hints: A palette on a core table is core's string and not the extension's. Add to it from Configuration/TCA/Overrides/ with ExtensionManagementUtility::addFieldsToPalette('tt_content', 'frames', 'my_field'), never by concatenating onto $GLOBALS['TCA']['tt_content']['palettes']['frames']['showitem']: the concatenation depends on the shape core happened to write — a trailing comma, line breaks, a label suffix per item — and core rewrites that shape between majors.

Where the string ends in no comma the appended item fuses with core's last one into an item naming no column, and PaletteAndSingleContainer skips an item naming no column without logging. So the core field at the end of the palette and the appended --linebreak-- both leave the backend form, no error is raised, and the stored rows are untouched. A field missing from a form after an override is that, a palette name core has changed, or a column the extension never declared with addTCAcolumns().

addFieldsToPalette() takes that shape apart itself. It trims the trailing comma and the whitespace off the existing string before joining, and drops from the insertion every field the palette already carries, so a second call adds the field once; --linebreak-- is exempt from that deduplication, so two overrides adding one each leave two line breaks. The fourth argument positions the insertion as before:<field>, after:<field> or replace:<field>, and where the palette carries no such field it is appended instead of refused. A palette that does not exist is created rather than refused too, and a palette no type's showitem names renders nowhere.

hints.text: The core's own showitem strings were rewritten on this branch: an item label is a short form reference where it was kept at all — starttime;core.db.general:starttime rather than an LLL:EXT: path — and tt_content's palettes lost their labels, their line breaks and the trailing comma two of them ended with. Extension code that appends to one of those strings, or matches a pattern in it, breaks on the upgrade to this branch and reports nothing. typo3_changelog_lookup with query "showitem" returns the breaking entry that lists what was replaced.

Appending to one of those strings works on this branch, which is what makes it the thing that breaks on the upgrade: core rewrites its own palette strings on the next major, and the field that disappears takes a core field with it.
typo3/sysext/core/Classes/Schema/ is the typed API over TCA. Ask TcaSchemaFactory for a TcaSchema and query it — fields, capabilities, relations, labels — instead of reading $GLOBALS['TCA'] directly.
A patch that reads TCA is increasingly expected to go through the schema rather than through the array; new code that touches record structure should not add a fresh $GLOBALS['TCA'] access.
The schema is cached per package set, so a change to how it is built is a functional-test change, not a unit-test one.

What the schema of one record type holds is a question of its own, and the answer is not "the table's columns": tca-sub-schema. A patch that swaps a table schema for a sub-schema without reading it drops every field the type's showitem does not name, and no core suite reports it.

title: What the Schema of One Record Type Holds

hints.text: A sub-schema holds the columns that record type's showitem names and nothing else. TcaSchemaBuilder::findRelevantFieldsForSubSchema() walks the showitem string, unpacks each --palette-- into the columns its palette names, drops --div-- tabs, and takes only what the columns section also declares. So a column that exists on the table and stands in no type's showitem is in the table schema and in no sub-schema, and code that resolves a field through the sub-schema stops seeing it.

That is the silent half. Core TCA puts its relation fields in showitem, so a change that resolves through the sub-schema instead of the table schema passes every core suite and drops the fields of any installation that does not. Where both are needed the two are unioned and each field resolved from the one that has it, rather than one replacing the other.

What the type may change is the field configuration and not the relations. columnsOverrides is merged over each column with array_replace_recursive, label first among what it changes, while the relation map is built once for the table and handed to every sub-schema — the builder says so where it passes it, and there is no per-type relation to read.

Whether a piece of core resolves through the sub-schema or through the table is a grep for getSubSchema over typo3/sysext/*/Classes/, and it is the reading that says whether a branch contradicts itself. DataHandler, FlexFormTools, RecordFactory, PageDoktypeRegistry and SearchableSchemaFieldsCollector are on the sub-schema side, and a class that writes or indexes records and is absent from that list is resolving fields the other way.

A table whose type is a field of another table has no sub-schema resolved from its own row. sys_file_reference declares ctrl type uid_local:type, SchemaTypeInformation::isPointerToForeignFieldInForeignSchema() is what asks, and RecordFactory and DataHandler skip the resolution where it answers true — the divisor sits in the foreign record, so reading it means reading that record. Code walking such a table row by row inherits that: resolving the type per row is a read per row.

title: FormEngine Data Providers
hints: FormEngine assembles its data through providers registered per form data group in $GLOBALS['TYPO3_CONF_VARS']['SYS']['formEngine']['formDataGroup']. The core declares the defaults in typo3/sysext/core/Configuration/DefaultConfiguration.php, but extensions add to them, so which groups and providers your installation really has is what typo3_configuration_lookup with path SYS/formEngine/formDataGroup answers.

Each provider maps to an array with 'depends' and 'before', both listing other provider classes. That graph is what orders the run, not the order the entries are written in — so the fix for a provider that sees stale data is usually an added dependency, not a change inside the provider class.
A provider that reads merged page TSconfig has to depend on PageTsConfigMerged, or it runs before the TSconfig it reads has been merged.
DefaultConfiguration.php is the default of TYPO3_CONF_VARS: an edit there changes behaviour in every installation, so say what changed and why in the patch description.
Registering or reordering a provider is a runtime-configuration change. It is covered by a functional test that renders the form data, not by a unit test of the provider in isolation.

title: What a Datetime Column Stores, and When It Is Null

hints.text: A TCA type=datetime field that is not nullable never holds SQL NULL. QueryHelper::transformDateTimeToDatabaseValue() writes 0 for an integer column and the empty literal for a native one — '0000-00-00' for dbType=date, '0000-00-00 00:00:00' for datetime, '00:00:00' for time.

DateTimeFactory::fromDatabase() maps that same empty value back to null on read. So a mapped property reading null does not mean the column is NULL, and a query for IS NULL does not find the row the object came from. That asymmetry is what a report of a query not finding its own object turns out to be.

Which value counts as empty depends on the column: for a non-nullable field it is the native literal where a dbType is set and 0 otherwise. A nullable native column additionally reads the legacy '0000-00-00' literal back as null, because rows written before it was nullable still carry it.

nullable defaults to false. DateTimeFieldType::isNullable() overrides that to true where a dbType is set, so a native date, datetime or time column is nullable unless the TCA says otherwise, while an integer column is not.
Before that override existed, DateTimeFieldType inherited isNullable() and the default was false for a native column as well.

Extbase omits a null property from the INSERT rather than writing NULL — Backend::insertObject() only fills a column where the property value is not null — so the column default decides what a new record stores. Reading it back through the factory then yields null again.

title: What an Inline Child Table Needs
appliesTo: child table on a normal page
child records in the wrong order
the drag order is not saved
hints: foreign_field is what makes the relation a child table rather than a list of uids: it names the column in the child that holds the parent uid, and the relation is read by querying the child for it. Without foreign_field and without MM the parent column stores a comma-separated list of child uids instead, and each child stays an ordinary record of its table with a lifecycle of its own.

foreign_table_field names the column in the child that holds the parent table name, and it is what lets one child table serve more than one parent table. It is written on save and added to the read query, so two parent tables sharing a child table without it read each other's rows wherever their uids collide.

foreign_sortby is one of four things that can order the children and it is not the required one. The read resolves foreign_sortby, then foreign_default_sortby, then the child's ctrl sortby, then its ctrl default_sortby; the write consults foreign_sortby and the child's ctrl sortby and nothing else. So a child with a ctrl sortby is ordered and re-ordered with no foreign_sortby at all, while a child carrying only a default_sortby reads in that order and the editor's drag persists nowhere.

The child rows sit on a page, and that page's type decides whether the table may be there. A folder takes any table; a standard page takes pages, sys_category, sys_file_reference and sys_file_collection, plus whatever the installed extensions have added to that list. security.ignorePageTypeRestriction in the child's own ctrl is how a table joins it, and without it DataHandler refuses the record and the new-record wizard does not offer the table.

hints.text: ExtensionManagementUtility::allowTableOnStandardPages() reaches the same list and is deprecated here, raising E_USER_DEPRECATED on every call. The ctrl key is what the next major reads.

hints: The workspace overlay belongs to the child table rather than to the relation: the read adds a workspace restriction only where the child declares versioningWS. A child without it is read live from inside a workspace, so a draft parent renders the published children.

type=file is this same relation with every key already filled in — sys_file_reference, uid_foreign, sorting_foreign, tablenames, and the field name as a match field. That is what a fully specified inline relation looks like, and it is why a file relation is declared as type=file rather than configured by hand.

This is what the parent field and the child table declare. What a relation looks like once it is written — the value the parent column takes, the NEW placeholders in it and when they resolve — is datahandler-relations.
